data.title: Hatné – Hrádok, the discovery of fragments of masonry architecture (P. Schreiber)
data.excerpt: The archaeologist Peter Schreiber reports on a fragment of a medieval mortared stone wall found on the rocky summit of Hrádok at Hatné, in the Marikovská valley. Until now the archaeological literature had assumed only a fortlet with a timber-and-earth structure at the site.
data.metaTitle: Hatné – Hrádok, a medieval stone wall discovered
data.metaDescription: The archaeologist Peter Schreiber on fragments of masonry architecture — a medieval stone wall — found on the Hrádok at Hatné in the Marikovská valley.

children.text: We bring you a new article by the archaeologist Peter Schreiber on the medieval stone wall discovered on the Hatné fortlet.

The village of Hatné lies in the Marikovská valley, in its lower part. There are two localities called Hrádok in the village, both long known as archaeological sites. Both localities consist of a limestone crag, with the Marikovský stream flowing between them.
The subject of this article is the Hrádok locality, which lies on the right-hand side of the Marikovský stream.
In 2016, during a familiarisation trip, Mgr. art. Ivan Pecháček drew attention to a fragment of stone masonry in the space between two rocks. The place lies within the rocky summit (fig. 3).

The fragment of wall is of coursed stone masonry 1.2 m long; a grey-white lime mortar was used as the binder (fig. 2). Fragments of mortar are also to be found on the rocky summit of Hrádok, from which it can be concluded that a building with masonry structures stood there, which is almost completely destroyed apart from the fragment of wall mentioned. On the slopes of the site in question there are likewise pieces of mortar, but also larger pieces of quarried stone with traces of lime mortar, in places scattered almost as far as the foot of the hill.

blocks.alt: Hatné – Hrádok, the discovery of fragments of masonry architecture (P. Schreiber)

children.text: The significance of the find of the fragment of wall and of masonry architecture lies in the fact that until now only a fortlet with a timber-and-earth structure had been assumed at the site in question in the specialist literature.

In Slovakia we know of fortlets with a single masonry tower, for example from Šípkov, or with a residential tower at Vajkovce (Plaček, Bóna 2007, 11). The first to mention the site in archaeological literature was Štefan Janšák, whose work also contains an illustration of it (Janšák 1930; fig. 1). From the High to the Late Middle Ages the site has yielded finds of pottery sherds, assigned broadly to the 11th to 13th century, and later finds dated to the 15th century (Malec 2009, 61, 62, 2010, 126; Moravčík 2002, 10; Španihel 2012, 61).

In the 15th century the historical sources mention the fairly important Hatňanský family (Fekete – Nagy 1941). They were a noble family of local origin and their original property was Hatné near Považská Bystrica (Marsina 1994, 91).

children.text: In 1430, for his part in the military campaign in Italy and for his services at the siege of the fortress of Golubac (in present-day Serbia), Ján Hatňanský received Budatín Castle from King Sigismund; his son Juraj is recorded in 1460 as castellan of Ilava Castle. Besides it he owned the villages of Hatné, Prosné, Klieština, Mariková and half of Kátlina (Šulavík 1991).

The historical importance of the Hatné site is also recorded in a later boundary survey (metatio) of 1664. It states that “the Vlachs owned the territory from the Bečva and Vsetín across the ridge of the Javorníky as far as the Hatné fortlets, where the Mariková church – called hrádok – is mentioned as the boundary”. On the map of the First Military Survey of Hungary in the 18th century there is, at the locality in question, a map symbol for a stone church with the inscription Rudera, which in translation means ruin (
). This is the second locality, on the left-hand side of the Marikovský stream.
